transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. [name]. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, I suppose what brings me in is that, for the past year or so, I just feel like I’m always puttering around. Fixing things, arranging, volunteering for just one more thing... You'd think at my age I'd be resting, but even at 87, I just have a very hard time sitting down and being still.

Over this past year, when you feel this need to keep moving and stay busy, would you say your mood has generally felt unusually upbeat, irritable, or 'wired,' or does it feel more like you're anxious or worried inside?

I wouldn't say it's any of those, really. I'm not a particularly worried or anxious person, and I don't feel unusually upbeat or irritable either. I'm just... my normal self, mood-wise. I just simply can't seem to sit in my chair and relax without needing to get up and do something.
Have you started or changed the dose of any medications recently, especially antipsychotic or anti-nausea drugs like haloperidol, risperidone, or metoclopramide?
No, I haven't started anything new. My medications have stayed exactly the same for quite a while now, and I definitely don't take any of those specific ones you just named.
Have you noticed any unintentional weight loss, feeling unusually hot or sweaty, a tremor in your hands, or your heart racing over this past year?

No, I haven't noticed any of that. My weight has been steady, and I don't feel hot or have any shaking in my hands. My heart feels fine, too. It's really just the restlessness, nothing else physical like that.
Do you notice any uncomfortable, crawling, or tingling sensations specifically in your legs when you're sitting or lying down, especially in the evening, that get better when you move them?

No, I haven't noticed anything like that. My legs don't tingle or feel uncomfortable, and it's not worse in the evening or anything. It's just a general feeling of needing to be doing something, not a physical feeling in my legs.
When you're trying to sit still, do you notice yourself repeatedly shifting your weight, rocking, or pacing back and forth, even without meaning to?

No, I don't really do that. I mean, I might shift around a little bit to get comfortable, like anyone else, but I don't catch myself rocking or pacing back and forth. It's just a feeling of wanting to be up and moving, but I don't do those specific things without meaning to.

If you're engaged in something you truly enjoy, like visiting with family or reading a good book, are you able to sit and stay still comfortably, or does the urge to get up and move persist even then?

Well, I'd say the urge is still there. Even if I'm having a nice time visiting with my family, or... or trying to read, I still feel like I need to get up after a little while. It doesn't really go away just because I'm enjoying myself. I just always seem to have that feeling that I should be up and doing something.
Does this need to keep moving ever interfere with your ability to fall asleep or stay asleep at night?

No, it doesn't really bother my sleep. Once I actually get into bed and decide it's time to sleep, I usually drift off fine. I don't wake up in the middle of the night feeling like I need to get up and walk around or anything like that. It's more of a daytime thing for me.
Do you regularly drink caffeinated beverages like coffee or tea, or take any over-the-counter medications or supplements that contain stimulants?

No, I don't. I gave up regular coffee and tea a long time ago, so I don't really get any caffeine that way. And I definitely don't take any over-the-counter pills or supplements like that, either. So no, nothing with stimulants.
Would you say this constant need to stay busy and moving is something new for you over the past year, or has this always been part of your personality throughout your life?

No, it's definitely not new. It's... well, it's just how I've always been, really, for as long as I can remember. I remember getting scolded back in grade school for popping out of my seat all the time. The teachers were always telling me I was talking over my classmates and that I was just... "too lively." That was long before I was even a teenager. So, yes, it's been a part of my life since I was a little girl.

latest_inference.note: Restlessness is lifelong, present since childhood, not related to mood change, medication, thyroid, RLS, or caffeine, and persists even during enjoyable activities without pacing/rocking - ruling out akathisia, RLS, hyperthyroidism, and general restlessness (R45.1), and pointing to a lifelong hyperactive-impulsive pattern consistent with ADHD.
